Background

I get a little weary as each influx comes in because I'm afraid that the community I've been a part of so long will be washed out by Reddit's lowest. As the latest (massive) wave came in a few days ago, I thought that this would be it for the little community we once had. The change is not as bad as I thought it would be, but there is a difference. Take these two threads as an example:

  • We are approaching 45.000 accounts : Posted 2015-05-26 (before the latest influx)
  • So we may be back up... : Posted 2015-06-12 (after the latest influx)

The difference I'm talking about is the ratio of insightful or informative comments to low-effort one-liner comments. I'm not one to mind the latter that much because I come here for fun, partially. However, I also come here to learn another thing about the world and Voat has been that vessel in most threads, even on the most popular subs.

My Point

* When I say the "decline in comment quality", I mean a "tip in the ratio scale", where most comments will either be non-serious jokes or serious, no-fun comments; I hold the opinion that the best community has a perfect mix of both.

Am I just seeing things with my bias? Is there any merit to my fears? Is this 'scale' I speak of arbitrary and non-existent?

I'd love to hear what the community thinks.

It seems to me that voat rewards new users for making "low-effort one-liner comments" since it allows you to get downvote/upvote privileges faster. I know it's supposed to encourage more quality content, but the whole system assumes that users will upvote the thought-provoking, well-researched, in-depth comment over the over-used joke comment, but that just doesn't happen.

I would blame that system for a decline in quality as a result of an influx of new users, but I don't disagree that it could also be the result of being "washed out by Reddit's lowest".

There was recently a great discussion on /r/theoryofreddit discussing the issue with the reddit ranking algorithm (I am brand new here, so I don't know whether I am allowed to link). But to your point, it inherently promotes low effort posts and comments. Vote-weighting for posts relies very heavily on the speed of the first 10 votes, so articles that are actually 'worth' reading lose out to links that are easily understood through the title. On the comment side, lengthy comments tend to get buried in larger subs because low effort comments get early upvotes and potentially better comments never get to compete. I don't know how the ranking system works on this site, but it would be interesting to see some of the ToR suggestions tried out while voat is still young... Maybe giving some flexibility to mods on how to curate their own front pages?

I would like to add a little bit of nuance to the discussion. I am new from Reddit myself and am enjoying the small community already.

As far as comment quality I think it is important to understand that the ability to have a serious discussion that involves critical thinking is a skill that is developed. Some people may not have had that skill nurtured growing up or in school. I know that in my high school in the U.S. the most popular kids were the ones with a 'don't give a shit' personality and did drugs and were rich. There is a very strong anti-intellectual attitude in schools. Now does that mean this sub should allow unintelligent comments, jokes, and inflammatory comments? No definitely not. So I think that moderators should understand that grammar, spelling, and lack of eloquence probably shouldn't be weighed all that much when deciding on quality of comment. I know on reddit some people's comments were dismissed based one spelling mistake and they were down voted.

Spelling isn't as big of an issue as perceived rightness based on popularity. This is why points should be hidden, and why I think a permanent (low) per-user cap needs be placed on how many votes can be given per day. It encourages discussion which can be defended, instead of encouraging votes which (invariably) makes dissent unseen. It is especially bad with perceived authority, such as academic or claims of prior experience. Part of critical thinking is accepting the possibility that someone with several Ph.D's can be horribly wrong, and someone without any of them can simply have had more interest in the subject without the opportunity. Even more importantly: Accepting the inability to be able to distinguish between the two and, thus, leaving well enough alone.

The nuanced social chaos behind why Reddit became awful is, sadly, something the people to blame have no patience to begin understanding. Which is, itself, the very cause of the issue.
I agree with your second point, the vote limit also helps bring lurkers out into the open, it gets people involved. That's what I think will set Voat apart, it has a community that is truly involved.
I think instead of having a vote limit, the CCP minimum for voting should be slowly raised as the user base grows.

Just my two cents as a new user:

This community, from what I've seen, values insightful and challenging discussion above pith and immaturity and, like showing up to a party full of strangers, it can be tempting to get a laugh right out of the gate to announce 'I'm here, I'm wacky, let's get to chuckling.' When that mentality is met with a less-than-expected reaction, though, any reasonable person will adjust accordingly to get the most out of their experience. From my scant time here, I've noticed that I'm seeing less reward for being zany or incongruous, which could be a result of the voting structure and a user base that's less receptive to meaningless antics. I'm optimistic that, as long as the desired tone and purpose of a place like Voat is maintained by folks who know what they really want, the quality of content will naturally err on the side of positive discourse and sharing interesting concepts and dialogue. Think 'invisible hand' but with pictures of cats.

As communities grow, quality will always decline. This may even be accelerated simply with new users joining. The quality decline will assist quality decline -- old users will get annoyed and leave and this will reduce the amount of quality posts being made even more. Really the only way to stop this in my opinion is through iron fist moderation -- although this very clearly goes against the idea behind Voat. What's more, is that it can stunt, or even reverse, community growth, especially if it is too harsh. User influx will be much less with stricter moderation, and users will leave inevitably anyway.

But I hope I'm wrong. I quite like Voat and I don't want it to die of expansion. But I don't want it to die from contraction or stagnation.

Oh well.
